final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep is easiest to control before anyone starts building. For a small business workflow, the decision is not “can AI do more?” but “what is the one recurring workflow we are fixing first?”

That is the boundary. In the diagnostic, I’d keep it to one repeatable workflow, one measurable outcome, and one fixed scope for the pilot. If the request starts widening into adjacent tasks, that is usually a sign to stop and separate the work, not quietly fold it into the current build. Otherwise the pilot becomes a moving target. Moving targets are a hobby, not a workflow.

A practical next step is simple: write down one weekly process that costs time or creates risk, and define how you will judge success in it. For example, customer questions answered within a set time, or invoices logged within a set window. Those are illustrations, not benchmarks.

Once that is written, the scope is visible before work starts. That gives you a cleaner decision: keep the current workflow bounded, or treat the extra request as a separate one for later. Human approval still stays with you.

critic_repairs.instruction: Rewrite the body into clear, grammatical English so the central point is easy to follow on first read. Keep the topic focused on one bounded workflow decision about scope creep, and make the next step explicit rather than buried in scrambled phrasing.

final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep is not just “more work.” In a small business workflow, it is the moment a useful pilot starts absorbing unrelated requests because the boundary was never written down.

The clean way to handle it is simple: pick one recurring workflow, define the one measure that matters, and make the scope explicit before build starts. Bareni’s normal sequence is a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal with fixed scope and price, then a paid working MVP. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees.

That matters because once the work starts, every new idea looks reasonable. Add invoice logging to a customer-support workflow, or a reporting request to an inbox workflow, and suddenly you are not refining a pilot anymore. You are designing a second workflow. That is where scope creep hides in plain sight.

So the practical next step is this: write down one weekly workflow that takes measurable time, and choose a success metric you can observe. For example, “customer questions answered within 2 hours” or “invoices logged within 24 hours.” Then use that as the diagnostic input. If a request does not fit that one workflow, park it for a later pilot.

The point is not to make the scope smaller for its own sake. It is to make the decision visible, so you can approve or reject it with your eyes open. A tidy boundary beats a heroic cleanup later.
